title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
description: Understand how to separate what a system must do from how well it must do it, and why both categories drive equally important architecture decisions.

data.text: Every software system has two kinds of requirements. Functional requirements describe what the system does: a user can place an order, a report can be generated, an email can be sent. Non-functional requirements describe how the system does it: the order must complete in under two seconds, the report must be available 99.9 percent of the time, the email must be encrypted in transit. Both are mandatory. Both constrain architecture. And confusing them is one of the most common sources of late-project surprises.

In a C# codebase, functional requirements usually map directly to methods, classes, and API endpoints. Non-functional requirements map to cross-cutting concerns: caching strategies, database indexing, async pipelines, logging infrastructure, and deployment topology. A senior engineer treats both categories with equal seriousness because non-functional requirements are often the ones that make or break a system in production.

data.title: Characteristics of functional requirements
items: Describe specific business behaviors and user interactions.
Can usually be tested as pass or fail with clear acceptance criteria.
Often expressed as user stories or use cases.
Map directly to features visible to users or external systems.
Examples: 'A user can reset their password,' 'The system sends a confirmation email.'

data.title: Characteristics of non-functional requirements
items: Describe quality attributes: performance, security, reliability, maintainability.
Often expressed as constraints, targets, or policies rather than features.
Harder to test directly; usually validated through load tests, audits, or benchmarks.
Apply to the system as a whole rather than a single feature.
Examples: 'The API must handle 1,000 requests per second,' 'Data must be encrypted at rest.'

data.title: The non-functional iceberg
data.text: Functional requirements are visible in the product; non-functional requirements are often invisible until they fail. A system can have every functional requirement met and still be unusable if it is too slow, too insecure, or too unreliable. Always document non-functional requirements explicitly and treat them as first-class constraints, not afterthoughts.
How Each Type Shapes C# Architecture

A functional requirement like 'generate an invoice PDF' leads you to choose a PDF library and design an Invoice service. A non-functional requirement like 'generate 500 invoices per minute' leads you to consider parallel processing, background queues, and memory management. In C#, the first is straightforward; the second requires understanding channels, background services, and resource pooling.

data.title: Functional requirement implementation
data.content: A straightforward service method that satisfies a functional requirement.

data.title: Non-functional requirement implementation
data.content: A background processing pipeline that satisfies a non-functional throughput requirement.

data.text: A frequent mistake is treating non-functional requirements as features. 'We need a caching layer' is not a feature request; it is a proposed solution to a performance requirement. The real requirement might be 'product search results must load in under 200 milliseconds.' Once that is stated clearly, you can compare in-memory caching, Redis, database indexing, or even a dedicated search engine like Elasticsearch.

items.question: Can a single requirement be both functional and non-functional?
items.answer: Rarely. If you can point to a specific button click or API call, it is functional. If it describes a quality attribute of the whole system, it is non-functional. Sometimes a requirement sounds like both ('the report must be exportable and complete in under 3 seconds'), in which case split it into two separate requirements.

items.question: Who is responsible for defining non-functional requirements?
items.answer: Product owners and stakeholders often state functional requirements. Non-functional requirements typically emerge from operations, security, compliance, or past incidents. A senior engineer should actively elicit them because they are easy to overlook until a production event forces the conversation.

items.question: How specific should non-functional targets be?
items.answer: Specific enough to measure and verify. 'Fast' is not specific. '95th percentile latency under 300ms during peak hours' is specific. Include the measurement window, the percentile, and the acceptable failure mode when the target is not met.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Functional requirements describe what the system does; non-functional requirements describe how well it does it.
Both categories drive architecture; non-functional requirements are often the harder constraint.
Treat non-functional requirements as measurable targets, not vague wishes.
Separate requirements from solutions; a 'caching layer' is a solution, not a requirement.
data.takeaway: A system that meets every functional requirement but misses its non-functional targets is still a failed system. Senior engineers give both categories equal weight from the very first conversation.
